# Winter Clothing Canada — Full Content (Mountain Warehouse & Columbia focus)

Winter Clothing Canada is an independent guide to winter clothing for real Canadian cold, focused on Mountain Warehouse and Columbia as of now. It sells nothing. Retailer links go to the retailers' own pages. No affiliate links are active yet; when added, they will be clearly marked. Updated November 4, 2026.

## Picks by job (research picks from published comparisons and reviews, not hands-on test winners)

- Best for deep cold on a budget: Mountain Warehouse Antarctic Extreme Waterproof Down Jacket. Laboratory tested to −40°C, 600 fill-power RDS down, waterproof to 5,000mm with taped seams and a fur-trim hood. Listed at $319.99 CAD at Mountain Warehouse Canada, November 4, 2026. Not best for ultralight travel — a heavy-duty winter jacket, not a packable layer.
- Best value everyday: Columbia Marquam Peak Fusion II Parka. Synthetic-insulated everyday parka with a hooded, longer silhouette, listed at $299.99 at Ernie's Sports Experts, price checked November 4, 2026. Not best for long inactive stretches at −30°C, where it needs a warm base layer underneath.

## Retailer listings

Mountain Warehouse Antarctic Extreme (men's), $319.99 CAD at Mountain Warehouse Canada — pros: −40°C lab testing, waterproof, RDS down, under $350; cons: heavy-duty cut, not packable, 5,000mm waterproof rating suits moderate rain, not storms. Mountain Warehouse Concord Extreme (men's), $189.99 CAD at Mountain Warehouse Canada — pros: lowest price on the page, long coverage, 3-year warranty; cons: long cut is not for everyone, same 5,000mm rating. Columbia Marquam Peak Fusion II (men's), $299.99 CAD at Ernie's Sports Experts — pros: easy-care synthetic fill, hooded longer cut; cons: synthetic fill is less warm per weight than down, not built for extreme exposure.

## Sweaters & layers

Wool, especially merino wool, is the warmest common sweater material because it insulates even when damp. Fleece is lighter, dries faster and is easier to care for, but is less warm for its weight. Cotton is the material to avoid in winter: it loses warmth when wet and dries slowly. In Canadian winters a sweater works as a midlayer: a moisture-wicking base layer underneath, the sweater for insulation, and a windproof, waterproof parka on top. Fit with room for a base layer underneath, without compressing the insulation.

## Buying guide

Down is warmer for its weight and packs smaller, but loses over 90% of its insulation when saturated with water. Synthetic is heavier and less warm per gram, but retains warmth when wet and dries faster. Fill power measures how much space one ounce of down fills, from about 550 to 900 cubic inches; higher fill power means better warmth-to-weight, not more warmth on its own. Temperature ratings are guides, not guarantees: brands do not share one standard, and warmth changes with activity level, wind, moisture and layering. Mountain Warehouse's −40°C figures are its own laboratory tests. The 3-layer system: moisture-wicking base layer, insulating midlayer, windproof and waterproof outer layer. At wind chill below −27, frostbite risk rises rapidly; at −28 to −39, exposed skin is at high risk within about 30 minutes (Environment and Climate Change Canada guidance).

## How we pick

What we do: start from published specifications; read professional reviews and user reviews, good and bad; compare by job, not by one winner; check real retailer listings with checked dates; state the limits (brand ratings are brand claims). What we do not do: no hands-on testing claims and no test scores; no fake reviewers; no copied content; no guessed links or prices; no fake certainty. As of now this page covers Mountain Warehouse and Columbia only; other brands will be added only with the same verification. If a price, specification or link is wrong, or if any retailer or brand asks for a listing to be removed, it is corrected or removed.
